research-water.body:
Water treatment becomes more challenging when organic pollutants and metal ions coexist and interact. EPA Lab investigates how oxidation and reduction can be coupled to connect pollutant treatment with resource recovery and energy generation.

We study interfacial charge transfer, integrated photoelectrochemical systems, and reactor designs that make more effective use of reactive species. Our [review of water oxidation and oxygen reduction](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.accounts.3c00002) explains how these reaction pathways underpin environmental photo(electro)catalysis.
research-water.researchDetails:
Organic pollutants and metal ions can coexist and form complexes in water, making their combined treatment difficult. EPA Lab investigates approaches that couple pollutant oxidation with reductive resource recovery. By controlling how photogenerated electrons and holes are transferred and used, we seek to connect water treatment with resource recovery and energy generation. Our [review of water oxidation and oxygen reduction](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.accounts.3c00002) describes how interfacial charge-transfer pathways determine pollutant transformation and the production of useful chemicals.

In a collaborative study, a solar photoelectrochemical system was developed to combine organic oxidation, uranium recovery, and electricity generation. Electrons obtained from organic oxidation were used to reduce uranyl ions, and the system was tested in complex water matrices, including real uranium tailings wastewater. This study shows how organic matter targeted for treatment can also serve as an electron source for resource recovery. [Coupled uranium recovery, organic oxidation, and electricity generation](https://doi.org/10.1002/adfm.202503925).

Another collaborative study introduced a gradient-driven, galvanic-enabled pathway for activating peroxymonosulfate (PMS) in a stacked flow reactor. The approach addresses oxidant utilization through the combined design of the catalyst and reactor, connecting reaction chemistry with continuous-flow water treatment. [Gradient-driven PMS activation in a stacked flow reactor](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.est.6c01180).

Our work on resource utilization also includes a review of the two-way relationship between biomass and photocatalysis: using biomass-derived materials to prepare photocatalysts, and using photocatalysis to convert biomass into useful chemicals and fuels. This review brings these approaches together and discusses remaining challenges in selectivity, stability, scalability, and economic viability. [Biomass for photocatalysis, photocatalysis for biomass](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.apcatb.2026.126768).

research-solar.body:
Absorbing light is only the first step in solar chemical production. Photogenerated electrons and holes must reach the right reaction sites before they recombine or enter competing pathways. EPA Lab designs catalyst structures and interfaces to improve charge utilization and control reaction selectivity.

Our studies examine [ultrathin MOF photocatalysts for hydrogen peroxide production](https://doi.org/10.1021/acsnano.4c11606), charge transfer at water-oxidation interfaces, and the relationship between oxide composition and catalytic behavior.
research-solar.researchDetails:
Even when a catalyst absorbs light, chemical production can be limited by charge recombination and competing reactions. EPA Lab investigates how catalyst thickness, defects, and interfacial structures influence the separation and transfer of photogenerated electrons and holes. These studies seek to direct charges toward useful chemical products and identify the mechanisms that govern reaction selectivity.

For hydrogen peroxide production, we designed approximately 1-nm-thick metal–organic framework (MOF) nanosheets integrating electron-donor and electron-acceptor components. This architecture promotes charge separation and couples oxygen reduction with water oxidation, producing hydrogen peroxide using water and dioxygen as the only reactant feedstocks. In oxygen-saturated water, the photocatalyst achieved an apparent quantum yield of 4.8% at 420 nm. The study demonstrates how an ultrathin structure and molecular charge-transfer design contribute to hydrogen peroxide photosynthesis. [Ultrathin donor–acceptor MOF nanosheets](https://doi.org/10.1021/acsnano.4c11606).

In a study of water oxidation, metal-incorporated carbon nitride films were deposited on hematite photoanodes. Spectroscopic and electrochemical analyses showed that the carbon nitride layer passivates the hematite surface and improves charge separation, while the incorporated metals facilitate hole transfer to interfacial water. This work explains why controlling surface losses and interfacial charge transfer is essential for improving photoelectrode performance. [Carbon nitride overlayers on hematite photoanodes](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.apcatb.2023.123167).

Our tungsten oxide study systematically varied oxygen content and oxidation state to investigate their effects on structure, electronic properties, and catalysis. Different compositions favored photoelectrochemical oxygen evolution or selective electrochemical oxygen reduction. The findings provide a framework for designing oxide structures and active sites around a desired oxidative or reductive reaction. [Tunable defect chemistry in nonstoichiometric tungsten oxides](https://doi.org/10.1021/jacs.5c20967).

research-air.body:
Air-pollutant treatment requires control over reaction products and sustained catalyst performance as well as removal rates. Oxygen, moisture, and the chemical identity of each pollutant can change adsorption, charge transfer, and reaction pathways.

EPA Lab investigates these processes to design pollutant-specific catalysts and reaction systems. Our work includes [oxygen-tolerant NO conversion to nitrogen](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-66008-z), light-driven organic pollutant mineralization, stored-charge CO oxidation, and collaborative studies of photothermal N₂O decomposition.
research-air.researchDetails:
Effective air-pollutant treatment requires attention to removal rates, reaction products, byproducts, and sustained catalyst operation. Oxygen and moisture can introduce competing reactions, while different pollutants require different conversion pathways. EPA Lab investigates pollutant adsorption, charge transfer, and surface chemistry to design catalysts and reaction systems that address these constraints.

For nitric oxide (NO), we incorporated C–F bonds into polymeric carbon nitride to suppress competing oxygen activation. Under visible light in simulated ambient air containing 20% oxygen, the catalyst achieved 85% NO conversion with 92% selectivity toward nitrogen (N₂). Mechanistic investigations connected selective NO adsorption and N–N coupling with the catalyst’s oxygen tolerance. This work demonstrates how surface bonding can direct NO toward nitrogen even in the presence of oxygen. [Oxygen-tolerant photocatalytic reduction of NO](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-66008-z).

For carbon monoxide (CO), we investigated oxidation that continues after a catalyst has been illuminated and the light is subsequently switched off. Oxidized platinum species were found to store long-lived electrons that support CO oxidation during the following dark period. The study shows that charge storage and the timing of charge utilization, alongside charge generation and transfer, can influence photocatalytic performance. [Preillumination-assisted CO oxidation](https://doi.org/10.1021/acscatal.5c07686).

For volatile organic pollutants, cyclodextrin-anchored tungsten trioxide enabled visible-light-driven acetaldehyde mineralization even under oxygen-free conditions. Spectroscopic and electrochemical analyses linked this behavior to interfacial charge-transfer complex formation and an extended charge-carrier lifetime. The study illustrates how modifying a catalyst interface can alter the conditions under which pollutant mineralization proceeds. [Oxygen-independent acetaldehyde mineralization](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.est.5c14689).

A separate collaborative study addressed volatile aliphatic amines using a triphasic system comprising tungsten trioxide, periodic acid, and an in situ surface water layer. Amine-specific reactions promoted carbon–carbon bond cleavage and rapid mineralization, while the surface water layer retained the ammonium product. This approach demonstrates the importance of matching reaction chemistry to the chemical properties of a target pollutant. [A triphasic photocatalytic system for amine mineralization](https://doi.org/10.1002/adfm.202528361).

In a collaborative study of nitrous oxide (N₂O) decomposition, isolated strontium atoms were incorporated into a nickel oxide lattice. The resulting Sr–O–Ni channels coupled light-driven electron excitation with thermally assisted surface reactions, facilitating N–O bond cleavage and oxygen recombination and desorption. This study provides an atomic-scale design strategy for linking charge transfer and oxygen dynamics in photothermal catalysis. [Single-atom channels for photothermal N₂O decomposition](https://doi.org/10.1021/jacs.6c05820).

research-ice.body:
Reactions measured in liquid water do not always explain how environmental substances behave when water freezes. Freezing can concentrate solutes and reactive components at ice grain boundaries, creating distinct chemical environments.

EPA Lab compares aqueous and frozen systems to investigate changes in oxidation state, reaction pathways, and product formation. Our [study of chromium chemistry in water and ice](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.est.5c09710), together with work on bromide and iodate, examines how freezing changes environmental redox processes.
research-ice.researchDetails:
Reactions observed in liquid water do not necessarily describe the behavior of environmental substances in frozen systems. As water freezes, some solutes and reactive components become concentrated at ice grain boundaries, creating distinct reaction environments. EPA Lab compares aqueous and frozen conditions to investigate how these changes affect oxidation states, reaction pathways, and the formation of environmentally relevant products.

In a collaborative study of bromide, oxidation by manganese oxide and the release of dissolved manganese occurred simultaneously in frozen solutions, although the coupled process was not observed in aqueous solutions. Concentration at ice grain boundaries was identified as a key factor. In the presence of fulvic acid, the formation of organobromine compounds also increased. These findings show how freezing can link halogen activation with changes in metal mobility. [Freezing-induced bromide oxidation and manganese oxide dissolution](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.est.4c07493).

Our iodate study found that photosensitized reduction by fulvic acid was substantially enhanced in frozen solutions compared with aqueous solutions. The process produced iodide, reactive iodine, and organoiodine compounds. This work identifies a pathway through which light and natural organic matter can alter iodine speciation in frozen environments. [Freezing-enhanced photoreduction of iodate](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.est.3c07278).

Our chromium study investigated how Cr(III)-bearing hydroxides can become a source of Cr(VI) under irradiation. Natural organic matter promoted Cr(VI) photoproduction in aqueous solution but inhibited it in frozen solution. These contrasting effects show that freezing does not influence every reaction in the same direction: its environmental consequences depend on the substances present and the pathways involved. [Chromium photooxidation in water and ice](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.est.5c09710).

040b80bb-8f69-49c4-b75b-046d442e4ac5.body:
Converting dilute CO₂ and NO into useful chemicals requires sufficient reactant delivery to an electrode and control over competing reactions. Low concentrations, limited mass transfer, and oxygen interference can restrict conversion.

EPA Lab designs gas diffusion electrodes that connect capture with conversion and investigates how local interfacial conditions govern catalytic pathways. Our work includes [dilute CO₂ conversion to formic acid](https://doi.org/10.1021/acsenergylett.5c03504), NO conversion to ammonium nitrate, and spectroscopic studies of CO₂ reduction on nanostructured gold.
040b80bb-8f69-49c4-b75b-046d442e4ac5.researchDetails:
Converting dilute carbon dioxide (CO₂) and nitric oxide (NO) into useful chemicals requires adequate reactant delivery to an electrode and control over competing reactions. Low reactant concentrations, limited mass transfer, and oxygen interference can restrict performance. EPA Lab designs gas diffusion electrodes that connect reactant capture with conversion and investigates how local chemical environments influence catalytic pathways.

For CO₂ conversion, a gas diffusion electrode was modified with porous graphitic carbon bearing oxygen and nitrogen functional groups. The modification enhanced CO₂ adsorption and suppressed oxygen permeation, enabling the conversion of dilute CO₂ to formic acid. Conversion was also demonstrated in oxygen-containing gas, and mechanistic and simulation studies examined how the functionalized carbon layer contributes to capture and oxygen tolerance. [Integrated capture and conversion of dilute CO₂](https://doi.org/10.1021/acsenergylett.5c03504).

For NO conversion, we developed gas diffusion electrodes that combine an NO-adsorbing MOF layer with a catalyst layer. An integrated cell coupled cathodic reduction with anodic oxidation to produce ammonium and nitrate ions from dilute NO gas. The study demonstrates how improving adsorption and mass transfer can connect air-pollutant capture with the production of useful nitrogen-containing chemicals. [Integrated electrocatalytic synthesis of ammonium nitrate](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-024-51256-2).

To understand interfacial mechanisms, we investigated CO₂-to-CO conversion on nanostructured gold using in situ infrared spectroscopy. The measurements revealed a locally alkaline environment and differences in the adsorption of reaction intermediates compared with an unstructured electrode. These findings explain how electrode structure affects the local reaction environment and pathways, informing electrode design alongside reactant-delivery strategies. [The local reaction environment on nanostructured gold](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.jpcc.3c02599).
